title: Hats and shared strategies
objectives: Design a team strategy for hat-colour puzzles using parity.

screens.title: Eight hats in a line
screens.prose: Eight people stand in a line, each seeing every hat in front. From the back, each calls red or blue aloud, hoping to name their own hat. Their code: person 8 says blue if he sees an even number of reds. The others then work out their own hats.
screens.question: What does each person call?

hints.text: Person 8 sees hats 1 to 7. Count the reds.
Four reds, an even number, so he says blue. Person 7 sees three reds in front.
The rest name their hats: R, B, R, R, B, B, R from person 7.

feedback.correct: B from the back, then R, B, R, R, B, B, R.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Person 8 follows the code; everyone else names their own hat.

byKey.r0c1: Person 8 sees 4 reds, an even number, so the code makes him say blue.
byKey.r1c1: Person 7 sees 3 reds and heard 'even'. So the fourth red must be his own.
byKey.r2c1: Person 6 sees 3 reds and heard one red call. That makes 4, even, so his hat is blue.

explain.text: Person 8 sees 4 reds and says blue, which is wrong for his own red hat. Person 7 sees 3 reds, so the even count needs his own hat red. Each later person adds the reds called behind to the reds in front, so all seven are right.

screens.title: Person 4's turn
screens.prose: Person 8 said blue: an even number of reds among hats 1 to 7. Persons 7, 6 and 5 then called red, blue and red. Person 4 sees hats 1 to 3.
screens.question: What is person 4's hat?

options.why: You counted only the red in front. Add the two reds called behind: 1 + 2 = 3, odd.
He knows the total is even and can count 1 red in front and 2 red calls behind.

hints.text: Among hats 1 to 7 the reds are even. Which of those does person 4 know?
He sees 1 red in front and heard 2 red calls behind.
1 + 2 = 3 reds known, so his own makes it even: red.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count reds in front and reds called behind, then make the total even.

byKey.blue: Reds known: 1 in front, 2 called behind. Three is odd, so his own hat is red.
byKey.cannot: The code plus the calls behind tell him everything except his own hat, and parity fixes that.

explain.text: Hats 1 to 7 hold an even number of reds. Person 4 knows 1 red in front and 2 red calls behind, which is 3. So his own hat is red: parity plus what he sees and hears settles it.

screens.title: Three colours
screens.prose: Now hats come in three colours, numbered 0, 1 and 2. Five people in a line, person 5 at the back. Person 5 calls the sum of the hats he sees, modulo 3. Each later person subtracts what they see and hear.

state.caption: Hats as numbers, front to back.

screens.question: What do persons 5, 4 and 3 call?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work modulo 3: call = announced sum minus what you see minus what you heard.

byKey.r0c1: Person 5 sees 0, 2, 1, 2, which sum to 5, and 5 leaves 2 modulo 3.
byKey.r1c1: Person 4 sees 0 + 2 + 1 = 3, which is 0 modulo 3. So his hat is $2 - 0 = 2$.
byKey.r2c1: Person 3 sees 0 + 2 = 2 and heard 2 from person 4. $2 - 2 - 2 = -2 \equiv 1$.

explain.text: Person 5 announces $5 \bmod 3 = 2$, his only free call. Person 4 sees 3, so his hat is $2 - 0 = 2$, and person 3 finds $2 - 2 - 2 \equiv 1$. With $k$ colours, the sum modulo $k$ plays the part of parity.

screens.title: All at once
screens.prose: Seven people wear hats numbered 0 to 6, and each sees all the others. Everyone guesses at the same moment. The code: person $i$ assumes the seven hats total $i$ modulo 7. He guesses the number that makes it so.

state.caption: People 0 to 6 and their hats. Person 4 sees every hat but his own.

screens.question: What number does person 4 guess?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $g$ with $20 + g$ leaving 4 on division by 7.

byKey.own: That is his real hat, which he cannot see. He guesses from the code.
byKey.sum: 20 is what he sees. He wants the total to leave 4 modulo 7.

explain.text: Person 4 sees 20 and needs a total of 4 modulo 7, so he guesses 5, which is wrong. The true total is 22, which leaves 1, so person 1 alone is right. The seven guesses cover all seven remainders, so exactly one person always is.

screens.title: Coin flips
screens.prose: Back to the line of 8 with red and blue hats. A candidate says each guess is a coin flip, so on average half the line is right.

state.caption: Hats from the front, person 8 at the back.

screens.question: How many of the 8 does the parity code guarantee?

options.why: You treated every call as a coin flip. Only person 8 guesses; the code lets the rest deduce.
That is what random calls give. The code makes 7 calls certain.
Person 8 has no information about his own hat, so his call is a coin flip.

hints.text: Which person has no information about his own hat?
The other 7 deduce, so 7 are certain.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the people who deduce rather than guess.

byKey.4: Calls are not coin flips under a code. Seven people deduce their hats.
byKey.avg4: Random calls average 4 right. The parity code guarantees 7.
byKey.8: Person 8 sees every hat but his own and hears nothing, so he cannot be sure.

explain.text: The coin-flip view assumes nobody shares information. Person 8 spends his call on parity, and the other 7 deduce their hats with certainty. Principle: one call can carry information for everyone else.

screens.title: A line of one
screens.prose: Edge case. A line of one person, with a red or blue hat chosen by a fair coin. He sees no hats and hears nothing.
screens.question: What is his chance of calling his own colour?

hints.text: None: no hats in front, no calls behind.
Any call is right with chance 1/2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With no information, any call is a fair guess.

byKey.zero: He might still be lucky: a call matches with chance 1/2.
byKey.one: A code needs someone to see a hat. He sees none.

explain.text: He is the back person and the front person at once, with nothing to see. A call matches his hat with chance 1/2. The code guarantees $n - 1$, which is 0 here.

screens.title: One call carries the code
screens.prose: Each time, one call carried a sum and everyone else subtracted. With $k$ colours numbered 0 to $k - 1$, the back person announces $s$ below. Person $i$ then calls $s$ minus what $i$ sees minus what $i$ heard, modulo $k$. $$s = \sum_{\text{hats seen}} h_j \bmod k$$ So $n - 1$ are certain.
screens.question: With 7 people guessing at once under the modulo 7 code, how many are right for every hat pattern?

options.why: Each remainder is claimed by one person, and the total has one remainder. So never two.
Someone always holds the true remainder, so the count never drops to 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The total has one remainder modulo 7, and each person claims a different one.

byKey.atleast: Two people would need the total to leave two remainders at once.
byKey.avg: The seven guesses cover all seven remainders, so one person is always right.

explain.text: Person $i$ is right exactly when the total leaves $i$ modulo 7. The total leaves one remainder, so exactly one person is right every time. A search of all $7^7$ patterns agrees.

screens.title: Drill: twenty in a line
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Twenty people in a line, red and blue hats, calling from the back.
screens.question: How many can a code guarantee?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. All but the back person can be certain.

byKey.20: The back person sees every hat but his own, so he cannot be sure.
byKey.10: That is random calling. The parity code does far better.

explain.text: The back person announces the parity of the reds he sees. The other 19 subtract what they see and hear, so all 19 are right. The back person is right with chance 1/2.

screens.title: Drill: twelve, three colours
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Twelve people in a line, hats in three colours, calling from the back.
screens.question: How many can a code guarantee?

hints.text: The back person calls the sum he sees modulo 3.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. One call carries the sum modulo 3.

byKey.12: The back person still has no information about his own hat.
byKey.4: That is a third, the random rate. The code guarantees 11.
byKey.10: One call is enough for three colours: the sum modulo 3 fits in one call.

explain.text: Number the colours 0, 1 and 2, and let the back person call the sum he sees modulo 3. Each other person subtracts what they see and hear, modulo 3. So 11 are certain.

screens.title: Drill: six in a line
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Six people, red and blue hats. The back person says blue if he sees an even number of reds.

state.caption: Hats from the front, person 6 at the back.

screens.question: What does each person call?

hints.text: He sees 3 reds, an odd number, so he says red.
The others name their own hats: 5 R, 4 B, 3 R, 2 R, 1 B.

feedback.correct: R from the back, then R, B, R, R, B.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Person 6 follows the code; the others name their own hats.

byKey.r0c1: Person 6 sees 3 reds, an odd number, so he says red.
byKey.r1c1: Person 5 sees 2 reds and heard 'odd', so his own hat is red.

explain.text: Person 6 sees 3 reds, odd, so he says red, which is wrong for his blue hat. Person 5 sees 2 reds, so the odd count needs his own red. The rest follow, and 5 of 6 are right.

screens.title: Drill: pass or guess
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Three players get red or blue hats by fair coins, and each sees the other two. All guess or pass at once; they win if someone guesses and nobody is wrong. Strategy: guess the opposite colour only if the two hats you see match.
screens.question: What is the team's chance of winning?

hints.text: In RRR and BBB everyone guesses wrong.
In the other 6, one player sees a matching pair and guesses right.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the patterns where the strategy wins.

byKey.half: That is one player guessing alone. The strategy wins in 6 of 8 patterns.
byKey.eighth: That is the chance of one pattern. The team loses in two, RRR and BBB, so it wins 6 of 8.
byKey.one: In RRR all three see a matching pair and guess blue, all wrong.

explain.text: In 6 of the 8 patterns, exactly one player sees a matching pair, and guesses right. In RRR and BBB all three guess wrong. So $6/8 = 0.75$, the best possible by a search of every strategy.

screens.title: Seven players, one code
screens.prose: Follow-up. The interviewer makes it seven players with the same pass rules. A strategy built on the Hamming code, an **error-correcting code**, loses only on its 16 codewords. There are $2^7 = 128$ hat patterns. The same codes guard data sent between trading systems.
screens.question: What is the team's chance of winning?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the losing share from 1.

byKey.75: That is the three-player answer. Seven players do better.
byKey.half: One player guessing alone wins half the time; the code does far better.

explain.text: It loses on 16 of 128 patterns, so it wins $112/128 = 7/8 = 0.875$. A check of all 128 patterns confirms it. Principle: pack all the wrong guesses into a few patterns, and pass everywhere else.

ideas: Agree a code in advance: one call carries the parity, or the sum modulo the number of colours.
Everyone else subtracts what they see and what they hear, so $n - 1$ are certain.
Guessing at once, person $i$ bets the total is $i$ modulo $n$, and exactly one is right.

formula.name: The back call
formula.note: Person $i$ calls $s$ minus what $i$ sees minus what $i$ heard, modulo $k$.

summary.trap: Calls under a code are not coin flips: the line of 8 is sure of 7, not half.

quiz.prose: Nine people in a line, red and blue hats. The back person says blue if he sees an even number of reds. He sees 5 reds.
quiz.question: What does he call?

options.why: Five is odd. The code says blue only for an even count.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Five reds is an odd count.

byKey.blue: Blue signals an even count, and 5 is odd.

explain.text: Five is odd, so he says red. His call carries parity, not his own colour. The eight in front then deduce their hats.

quiz.prose: Four people in a line, hats numbered 0, 1 and 2. The back person calls the sum he sees modulo 3. He sees 2, 2 and 1.
quiz.question: What does he call?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add what he sees, then take the remainder on division by 3.

byKey.five: 5 is the sum; the call is its remainder modulo 3.

explain.text: $2 + 2 + 1 = 5$, and 5 leaves 2 on division by 3. So he calls 2. The three in front then subtract what they see and hear.

quiz.prose: Seven people, hats numbered 0 to 6, all guessing at once. Person $i$ assumes the total is $i$ modulo 7. The hats total 30.
quiz.question: Which person guesses right?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the remainder of 30 on division by 7.

byKey.thirty: People are numbered 0 to 6. Take 30 modulo 7.

explain.text: $30 = 28 + 2$, so the total leaves 2 modulo 7. Person 2's assumption is the true one, so he alone guesses right. Every other person is wrong.
